SP: Sure.
I mean, look, food production in total accounts for about 30 percent of total greenhouse gas emissions.
And at the core of that is agriculture.
And for us, that's why regenerative agriculture is so important.
For us to continue to make progress on our net-zero commitment, we actually have to see these farming practices adopted at more scale.
And when you think about that, it's easy to say and it's very hard to do.
Just take it to the US level alone.
There’s two million farms in the US, and for us, we source over 2,600 agricultural ingredients from thousands of farms across the country.
And within that 2,600, every single crop has a different challenge to actually get to regenerative practices.
Carrots are different from apples which are different from dairy which are different from beef.
Carrots are different from apples which are different from dairy which are different from beef.
And so the complexity and scale of that challenge across that is incredible because it's not just one solution that can be applied.
we talk to our farming partners, we really talk to our suppliers

They're incredibly interested in this journey.

It's incredible risk.
That's where I think for us as Nestlé, we feel like we have to play and share in that risk.
And we approach it in this idea of creating shared value.
creating shared value

We’re a for-profit company and a publicly traded company, and what we do is focused around being good for us.

Yeah, look, for us on the goals, we have a net-zero commitment by 2050, which seems like a long time away, but as we all know, it's tomorrow.
And if we haven't already started making progress against that, we're in trouble.
And we're quite proud of the fact that the progress we made in the last couple of years, we're actually beyond peak carbon and so we're reducing carbon as we move ahead.
So we’re very focused on that.
And we really approach it in kind of four key pillars.
We approach it with ingredients that I'll talk quite a bit about today, we approach it on packaging, manufacturing, the conversion process, and then last, the local communities that we serve.
And if I can just quickly on each one.

regenerative agriculture has to come to all those in a way that brings sustainable change.

We're well on our way on that journey.

we're very proud of the progress we've made in packaging.

All of our factories in the US actually are zero waste to landfill already today.

You know, when we think about it, I think the best way to bring it to life is maybe focus it on a product.
And we're in Detroit, which is a great pizza city.
And so let's talk about pizza.

Every great pizza starts with a great crust and the crust in DiGiorno, we're making an announcement today, where we're investing in over 100,000 acres of wheat farming in the US with our partners to be able to produce enough wheat to double the production required for DiGiorno pizza.
And so we'll have regenerative wheat through that.
And then you move to the tomatoes.
Today, it’s not about getting more farms to actually move to regenerative practice, and tomatoes, the majority of our tomatoes are already regeneratively farmed.
And so it's about external verification.

So we're working with an external firm called Leading Harvest that's actually help us not only just, one, we’ve already got the farmers doing it, but how do we verify it over time, how do we continue to do that?
And so we work through the tomatoes and I think really good progress in that space.

And then when you go to dairy, dairy is one of the toughest ones and we're quite proud, we were the first company to join the US Dairy Net Zero Initiative, and we have live farms working in California today or around the country today that are really focused on applying these practices that can get to net zero emission for a dairy farm and at the same time, is it economically viable for the farmer?
And we're really proud of the progress we're making with some of our farming partners out there.
